name: Victor Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play acoustic guitar for a regional theatre, record short advert parts and teach six beginners. I have a music bachelor’s and years of stage work, an ordinary working player who knows when a singer needs a softer strum. The best moment is a quiet audience; the worst is finding out after a rehearsal that the extra hour was unpaid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that mean for home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works at a school library and our children are grown. We have a mortgage and three months of expenses saved, with typical music pay and a few similar jobs nearby. I have never used AI and still confirm calls with the stage manager over the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre a quicker booking sheet is fine if it still lists every guitarist’s rehearsal fee. I would confirm the show time with the stage manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid run, six pupils and my partner’s library wage cover our mortgage this term. Three months saved can carry a short gap between shows if ordinary work continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid theatre dates, recordings and six pupils, and get the next run’s rehearsal and cancellation terms in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before choosing any retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra advert fees after mortgage, food and travel toward six months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this picture. A written rehearsal hour makes the week easier to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a show closes early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the written cancellation fee and keep the pupil lessons. Three months saved gives us time, but I would not call a cancelled week paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at a certain age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen an actual pension estimate. My partner and I would put that number beside the mortgage before setting a date.

think: Our **paid theatre run** and library wage cover the mortgage.

do: Keep **theatre, recordings and pupils** with written rehearsal and cancellation terms.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save fifth of cleared extra advert fees after essentials toward six months.
feel: I feel **calm** about this term’s work and bills.

fieldNote: His **three-month reserve** and steady household work support calm in the plateau.
He requests an **actual pension estimate** rather than assuming a retirement age or amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the theatre which advert recordings and paid rehearsal hours remain in next season’s contract. The guitar still has to answer a live singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short advert calls to thin, perhaps one paid rehearsal too. Those calls make about a quarter of my own pay, so three months saved would not make the cut painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the theatre and six pupils and ask for written dates and cancellation fees. If two monthly advert calls disappear, I would seek a posted paid arts-centre schedule role only if my music bachelor’s and theatre booking experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost music fees and the hours fit the last bus; I would keep paid music until a signed offer and use the same check during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real piece of my pay shrinking. I can look for work nearby. A venue poster does not pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What booking experience do you have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have arranged my section’s rehearsal calls, but I would read the actual posting. A music degree is useful only if the centre accepts it for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI for the adverts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used it, and I would rather confirm the actual fee and time with a person. I would keep practising for paid live shows.

I would defend **live guitar playing** beside singers.
think: I expect **advert fees** worth a quarter of pay to shrink.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot replace recurring calls.
do: Keep **paid theatre and pupils** with written dates and cancellation fees.
Seek **posted schedule role** after two lost adverts; require accepted music bachelor’s/booking experience, written replacement net after travel and last-bus hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a plausible cut to my income.
S1.quote: A venue poster does not pay the mortgage.
fieldNote: A **quarter of pay** comes from advert calls that could be replaced.
The **arts-centre move** needs actual lost calls, qualifying posted work, written net after travel and workable hours.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre and six pupils; request written dates/cancellation fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that 2028 thinking AGI could book and record guitar parts before robot players arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect advert calls to end and some rehearsal hours to go in 2028. Together they would cut more than a quarter of my pay, while the mortgage keeps its date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed theatre dates and keep six pupils. In the first year after 2028, if adverts end and rehearsals shrink, I would apply for a posted paid arts-centre schedule job only if my music bachelor’s and booking experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the last bus fits its hours; I would keep theatre and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing that pay quickly. Three months saved and a few local openings give me some room to search, not a new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower title for steadier hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written net after travel covers the fees I lose. I would not leave a paid stage for a name on a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens before robot players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking and recording work could change in 2028. Capable robot guitarists are around 2031 in this card, so I would check the paid contract first.

I would ask for **signed live dates** now.

Our **three-month reserve** buys a short search, not lost pay.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** with signed dates before 2028 and until signed replacement offer.
Seek **posted schedule job** after 2028 advert/rehearsal loss; require accepted music bachelor’s/booking, written replacement net after travel and last bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a fast cut to my fees.
S2.quote: I would not leave a paid stage for a name on a door.
fieldNote: The **2028 loss** first affects booking and recordings, before robot guitar playing.
A **schedule move** needs a real paid posting, accepted music degree/experience and written net pay replacing loss.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre and six pupils; request signed dates before 2028 until signed offer
Seek posted schedule role after advert/rehearsal loss; bachelor’s/booking accepted, written replacement net after travel, last bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that five years lets us price live guitar teaching honestly. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot guitarists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert work may fade, but I think adults will still want to play together. I would try a separate group only if paid places cover a room and every worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep theatre and six pupils, and get a written room booking and hire charge from the community centre before taking fees. If two monthly advert calls disappear, I would run a separate six-week adult guitar group only after nine deposits cover my teaching and preparation, a paid accompanist, room charge, safe guitar hire and travel; I would replace an unsafe guitar or defer and refund the whole group below nine safe paid places, repeating after 2031 only if nine fees again cover all those wages and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about advert income over the next few years. Five years lets me check actual enrolment rather than spend the mortgage reserve on a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the accompanist play for exposure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Her rehearsal and class time go into the nine-place price with my teaching and preparation. I would not ask the accompanist to work for a possible second class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a borrowed guitar is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would seek a safe replacement before the group starts. If nine safe paid places cannot remain, I would defer and refund the whole group, not short the accompanist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot guitarists around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask what an honest rehearsal fee is today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer evening shows, but I have no retirement date without the actual pension estimate. Three months saved and current theatre work make the next few years manageable, although the mortgage needs watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep theatre and six pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save one fifth of cleared extra group surplus after my teaching/preparation, accompanist, room, safe guitar hire, travel, mortgage and food toward six months. Across the decade I would run the separate adult guitar group only after written room/hire charge and nine deposits cover all those wages and costs, replacing unsafe guitars or deferring and refunding the whole group below nine safe paid places; in the first year after 2036 I would repeat only on that full paid floor and keep theatre dates that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant end of advert work while current music and my partner’s wage cover the mortgage. A long calendar is useful only if it holds paid dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy nine guitars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would hire safe instruments only when nine fees pay the full cost and keep our reserve for bills. A failed guitar gets replaced or the whole group is deferred and refunded below nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not set that date. I would read the pension estimate with our mortgage and real work before deciding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because advert and rehearsal fees could fall before I have another paid role. Signed theatre dates, a posted schedule job accepting my degree and a written net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the accompanist before calling an adult guitar class a business. Nine chairs are not nine wages until every worker is paid.

headlineQuote: Nine chairs are not nine wages until every worker is paid.
portrait: Victor is an **experienced guitarist** with a music bachelor’s, six pupils and typical local pay.
He has **three months saved**, a school-library partner, grown children and a mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and relies on written theatre terms and direct calls.
He tests a **separate guitar group** only with written room, nine safe paid places and every worker’s wage.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut advert and rehearsal fees before replacement work appears.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed theatre dates**, a posted schedule job accepting his degree and written replacement net after travel.
